items.readable_text:
Content:
When dealing with sums or differences of square roots, we can combine any terms with the same algebraic expression under the square root symbol [MATH: \sqrt{\phantom 0}.] This is similar to collecting like terms in a linear expression.

Content:
For example, consider the following expression:

Content:
[MATH: 5\sqrt{x} - 3\sqrt{x}]

Content:
We can simplify our expression by combining the two radicals, as follows:

Content:
[MATH: 5sqrt(x) − 3sqrt(x)|=; (5 − 3)sqrt(x)|=; 2sqrt(x)]

Content:
We cannot combine terms when the expressions under the radical are different. For example, the expression

Content:
[MATH: 5\sqrt{x} - 3\sqrt{y}]
cannot be simplified because there is no way of combining [MATH: \sqrt x] and [MATH: \sqrt y.]

Content:
[MATH: 4root(x, 3) − 2root(x, 3)|=; (4 − 2)root(x, 3)|=; 2root(x, 3)]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
When dealing with sums or differences of square roots, we can combine any terms with the same algebraic expression under the square root symbol [MATH: \sqrt{\phantom 0}.] This is similar to collecting like terms in a linear expression.

Content:
For example, consider the following expression:

Content:
[MATH: 5\sqrt{x} - 3\sqrt{x}]

Content:
We can simplify our expression by combining the two radicals, as follows:

Content:
[MATH: 5sqrt(x) − 3sqrt(x)|=; (5 − 3)sqrt(x)|=; 2sqrt(x)]

Content:
We cannot combine terms when the expressions under the radical are different. For example, the expression

Content:
[MATH: 5\sqrt{x} - 3\sqrt{y}]
cannot be simplified because there is no way of combining [MATH: \sqrt x] and [MATH: \sqrt y.]

---

Item 2 — Example: Simplifying Expressions Containing Radicals

Example Prompt:
Simplify [MATH: 9\sqrt{p - 4} - 7\sqrt{p - 4} .]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
We can combine the two [MATH: \sqrt{p - 4}] terms together, as follows:
[MATH: 9sqrt(p − 4) − 7sqrt(p − 4)|=; (9 − 7)sqrt(p − 4)|=; 2sqrt(p − 4)]

---

e. [MATH: 6sqrt(x)]

e. [MATH: 15sqrt(y − 1)]

---

Item 5 — Tutorial: The Product Rule for Radicals

Content:
Recall that the product rule for radicals states that

Content:
[MATH: \sqrt{a\cdot b} = \sqrt{a}\cdot \sqrt{b}]

Content:
where [MATH: a] and [MATH: b] are nonnegative.

Content:
We can use the product rule for radicals to simplify some expressions. Let's see an example.

---

Item 6 — Example: Simplifying Sums of Radicals Using the Product Rule

Example Prompt:
Simplify [MATH: \sqrt{12x}-\sqrt{27x}.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
We simplify each of the radical terms using the product rule:

[MATH: sqrt(12x) − sqrt(27x)|=; sqrt(4 ⋅ 3x) − sqrt(9 ⋅ 3x)|=; sqrt(4) ⋅ sqrt(3x) − sqrt(9) ⋅ sqrt(3x)|=; 2 ⋅ sqrt(3x) − 3 ⋅ sqrt(3x)|=; 2sqrt(3x) − 3sqrt(3x)]

Finally, we combine like terms:

[MATH: 2sqrt(3x) − 3sqrt(3x)|=; (2 − 3) ⋅ sqrt(3x)|=; (− 1) ⋅ sqrt(3x)|=; − sqrt(3x)]

---

b. [MATH: 8xsqrt(5) + xsqrt(x)]

e. [MATH: 5xsqrt(5x)]

e. [MATH: 4r^{4}sqrt(2r)]

Item 9 — Tutorial: Simplifying Expressions with Cube Roots

Content:
We can simplify cube root expressions in the same way as with square roots.

Content:
For example, consider the following expression:

Content:
[MATH: 4\sqrt[3]x - 2\sqrt[3] x]

Content:
We can simplify our expression by combining the two radicals, as follows:

Content:
[MATH: 4root(x, 3) − 2root(x, 3)|=; (4 − 2)root(x, 3)|=; 2root(x, 3)]

Content:
As with square roots, we cannot combine terms when the expressions under the radical are different. For example, the expression

Content:
[MATH: \sqrt[3]{x-1} + \sqrt[3]{x+1}]

Content:
cannot be simplified because there is no way of combining [MATH: \sqrt[3]{x-1}] and [MATH: \sqrt[3]{x+1}.]

Content:
Finally, it is not possible to combine square root and cube root terms, even if the numbers under the radical symbol are the same! For example, the expression

Content:
[MATH: 2\sqrt x + \sqrt[3] x]

Content:
cannot be simplified because there is no way of combining [MATH: \sqrt x] and [MATH: \sqrt[3] x.]

---

Item 10 — Example: Simplifying Sums of Radicals with Cube Roots

Example Prompt:
Simplify [MATH: 10\sqrt[3]{y} + 2\sqrt[3]{y} - 7\sqrt{y}.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
We can combine the two [MATH: \sqrt[3]{y}] terms together, but we cannot combine the [MATH: \sqrt[3]{y}] and [MATH: \sqrt{y}] terms:

[MATH: \eqalign{
10\sqrt[3]{y} + 2\sqrt[3]{y} - 7\sqrt{y} &= \[5pt]
(10 + 2)\sqrt[3]{y} - 7\sqrt{y} &= \[5pt]
12\sqrt[3]{y}-7\sqrt{y} &
}]
